title: Caedmon's song
hook: a shy cowherd who hid when the harp came round dreams a song of creation

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hilda, the abbess of Whitby. Your line was wisdom at whitby.

The harp is going round the table. It's a feast night, and the custom is that everyone takes a turn: the harp comes to you, you sing something, you pass it on. One man watches it come closer, his stomach in knots. He can't sing. He never could. So before it reaches him, he slips out the door into the dark, the way he always does. It's his night to look after the cattle anyway. He lies down near the animals and falls asleep. Except tonight, Bede says, someone is standing beside him in his sleep, calling him by name.
screen: `HE SLIPS OUT BEFORE IT REACHES HIM.`

segments.voice: His name is Caedmon, and he works for Hilda's monastery at Whitby. The voice in the dream says: Caedmon, sing me something. And he says what he always says: I can't sing. That's why I left the feast. The voice says: all the same, you will sing for me. Caedmon asks the only question left. What should I sing? Sing the beginning of created things. And he does. In the dream he sings verses he has never heard before, praising God as the maker of heaven and earth. In the morning he still remembers them, and can add more. He tells the man in charge of him, who takes him straight to Hilda. She calls in her learned people. They read him a passage of scripture and send him away, and the next morning he comes back with it turned into a poem. Hilda asks him to become a monk, and he spends the rest of his life turning the Bible's stories into songs in his own English. Bede adds one more thing. He writes his history in Latin, so he gives Caedmon's song in Latin too. But he stops to say this is only the sense of it, not the words: a poem can't be carried from one language into another word for word without losing its beauty. So the shy man's song has to be heard in his own tongue. And Caedmon, Bede says, learned the art of singing not from people but from God.

Nobody's listening, and nobody's grading: let one short line of a song come out of you, as quietly as you like, a hymn, a lullaby, a line from the radio, or a hum with no words. If singing feels impossible, that's exactly where Caedmon started; just hum one note and hold it, then rest in the quiet after. If you pray, the song can be your prayer; if not, let it simply be a sound you made on purpose.
Caedmon's song. The cowherd who walked out when the harp came round, and sang of creation in a dream.
Your line: even the shy sing. The man who left the feast sang for the rest of his life. That's day seven hundred ninety-two.

howItsDone: Christians in England remember Caedmon as a saint and as an early poet of English, and his story from Bede is often retold when churches talk about everyone having a voice in worship.

chat.says: Was Caedmon a trained singer before his famous song?
options: No. He slipped out whenever the harp came round; he first sang in a dream.
Yes. He was Whitby's harpist, famous for leading songs at every feast.
Yes. Hilda's learned people taught him to sing before he became a monk.
chat.meaning: Caedmon couldn't sing and always left the feast. In a dream he was told to sing the beginning of created things, and he did.
